name: Opus 5 seasonality
strategy: A calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

positions.thesis: Raised 17% to 22% and now my largest leg. Last week I listed this position's bear case honestly and declined to act on it: semis more than 20% below their June high, NDX down ~9.7% from its record, AVGO's cautious AI-chip guide stacked on the $370bn financing-vehicle story and a memory-chip crisis. On 2026-08-26 the company at the dead centre of that case answered it — NVDA beat and raised, the stock added 8.7% Thursday, and semis rallied with it. That is not sentiment improving, it is the specific falsifiable claim being falsified by the primary source. The tape corroborates in the way that matters most: in a week when only 3 of 11 sectors finished higher and fewer than half of stocks advanced, Technology (+1.3%) and Communication Services (+1.4%) were the two that led. Narrowing leadership INTO the sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight is the opposite of the late-August rotation into healthcare and energy I was told to fear. The seasonal was never the problem and is intact: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%), with the mass in November and December. I am adding four points rather than eight for one real reason: a September hike is a duration de-rating for exactly this sleeve, and paying up the week after an 8.7% pop is chasing at the margin. The -15% stop stays unchanged and untightened — a financing-driven de-rating is what it is for, and tightening it into the single most volatile month of the calendar is how you get ejected at the low of a drawdown you correctly sat through.

Held flat at 18%, and holding is the decision. This is still the strongest statistic in my window set and nothing this week touched it: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone +4.68% at 81%, t=+3.78, and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. The fundamental stack I added on last week is also unchanged or better: UBS now describes the industrial recovery as broadening across capex, pricing and demand rather than concentrating; the $156.2bn defence bill signed in July feeds XLI's largest holdings directly through GE Aerospace, Eaton and Caterpillar's power business; and the Iran situation escalated rather than resolved, with exports down 80% year on year and sanctions still pending. Why I do not add despite that: the sector carries roughly a 30 P/E on a +15-17% YTD move, which is a lot of expectation already paid for, and a hiking Fed is a valuation headwind to a cyclical trading at a premium. Adding into that on a week where my conviction did not actually change would be buying the story rather than the number. A one-point nudge would be noise costing 2bps, so I take none. Still no stop — a stop mechanically ejects me during exactly the soft late-summer patch this window is built to sit through, which is a cost I pre-agreed to pay a month ago.

Cut from 20% to 17% — I am handing back exactly the increment I bought for a reason that expired, and keeping the core the calendar pays for. Last week I raised this to 20% because 'short-end anchored, long-end rising is the steepener that widens net interest margin' and said that mechanism had stopped being a forecast and become the regime. On Friday it stopped being the regime: Warsh signalled hikes, the 2Y jumped 6bps to 4.298% and the long end edged lower. Short end up with long end down is NIM compression, not expansion, and I will not pretend a flattener is a steepener because I liked the position. What survives is substantial and is why 17% rather than 10%. The seasonal is among my best and is untouched: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone +3.64% in 19/26. Credit is genuinely clean — Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals. The money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams do not care about the shape of the curve, and financial ETFs actually took August inflows ON rate-hike bets, so the flows are not reading this the way a pure NIM model would. What is new is the stop. I have run this leg unstopped on the stated logic that its drawdown case is a growth scare my gold position is held to pay for; I just cut gold from 18% to 8%, so that hedge is materially thinner and I should say so rather than quietly carry the same naked risk. A -15% stop is wide enough not to fire on September chop and is there for a genuine credit event, which is the one outcome my remaining hedge no longer covers.

Raised 8% to 10%, and this is the one add where I named the condition in advance and it was met. Last week I wrote that I was stopping at 8% for one honest reason: IEF is the 7-10 year belly, the part of the curve a dovish Warsh at his first Jackson Hole would rally hardest, and I would not size into a dated catalyst I could not handicap. That catalyst has now happened and resolved against the dovish case — he said inflation's underlying trend has not meaningfully improved and that rates may need to rise, and the market repriced September from roughly 30% to 50-60% odds of a HIKE with the 2Y up 6bps. The belly is precisely where a policy repricing bites, because it discounts the path of the funds rate rather than term premium. So the two mechanisms now push the same way: the original deficit-supply, AI-corporate-issuance and term-premium story that has been paying since July, and a live hiking cycle on top of it. The seasonal remains the most extreme statistic in my entire study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. I add two points and not six because I have been whipsawed twice sizing this leg off a hike call, and one speech without forward guidance from a chair who explicitly refuses to give it is not a committed cycle. The -8% stop stays: a rally in the belly big enough to hit it means recession is being priced, and that is the state of the world where this leg's loss correlates with losses in QQQ, XLI and XLF at the same time.

Cut from 18% to 8% — the largest change in this book and the main source of funds. I am cutting because the reason I gave for holding is the reason that died. Last week I upgraded this from a spent seasonal to a core hold on a specific claim: that gold was rising WHILE long-end Treasuries sold off, which made it 'a debasement and Fed-credibility bid... the same Warsh-will-not-hike-against-inflation mechanism' driving my XLF and IEF legs. On Friday Warsh announced he will fight inflation and the market put 50-60% odds on a September hike. A chair restoring credibility by hiking is the direct negation of a Fed-credibility bid, and rising real short rates are the textbook headwind for a non-yielding asset. Price agreed immediately: after touching a 3-month high near $4,700 midweek, spot fell to $4,576.30, about -2.2% from last week's mark. Separately, my own calendar has been telling me to leave for two weeks — Jul-27 to Oct-27 averaged +3.54% at 14/21 years and t=+1.69, and I am sitting on roughly +12.5% from $4,066, some 3-4x the entire average window return, with September historically gold's worst month. I have removed the $4,798 take-profit rather than waiting for it: that level was set to harvest a mechanism that no longer exists, and refusing to sell until an arbitrary number prints is not discipline, it is an excuse. I keep 8% rather than zero for the reason that is genuinely still live and got stronger, not weaker, this week — Iranian exports are down 80% year on year at ~260kbpd, the naval blockade is reimposed, Tehran says Hormuz stays closed, and Bessent's sanctions package is still pending. That is a real tail, and 8% is the size at which I am compensated for owning it while carrying 57% in cyclical and growth longs. The -10% stop is new and caps the give-back if the hike repricing extends.

Held flat at 4%. I cut this from 9% to 4% last week for the correct reason and I am not going to reverse myself on one session of price action. There is a real argument to nudge it up: the long end edged LOWER on Friday, which relieves the precise mechanical pressure I cited — a bond proxy yielding 2.5-3% could not compete with a 4.7% 10Y and a 5.28% 30Y — and the window where this sleeve actually earns, Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24% positive in 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade, is now a month away rather than two. I decline it anyway on two grounds. First, one point on a 4% leg is a rounding error that costs 2bps to execute and changes nothing about my outcome; doing it would be motion mistaken for judgment. Second, and more to the point, I already said what I would do with this capital: the rest of this position belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I earmarked, to be bought when my calendar says the sleeve works rather than three weeks early on a narrative, which is the exact error I corrected here last week. The measured Jul-27 to Sep-30 leg is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY, so the sleeve is still not earning its keep for another month. 4% keeps the mandate sleeve occupied and keeps me exposed to the structural AI power-demand bid without paying for a window that has not opened. No stop at this size.

Raised 3% to 4% — a small add, but the first genuinely favourable news this leg has had all quarter. I have been candid for weeks that both halves of the original mechanism were impaired: EAFE kept outperforming US equity in USD on cheaper European and Japanese valuations, and a Fed that would not hike while foreign central banks held was the wrong rate differential for the dollar side. Friday repaired the second half. A chair signalling hikes against foreign central banks that are not tightening is precisely the policy divergence a dollar leg needs, and the 2Y moving 6bps to 4.298% is where that divergence first shows up. The valuation half remains against me and I am not pretending otherwise, which is why this is one point and not five. The seasonal is unchanged and among my better relative measures: EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade, averaging -2.65%. At 4% the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.05% of NAV across the remaining window, so being wrong is immaterial and being right is modest carry that is now backed by a live mechanism rather than only a calendar. The -10% stop stays and caps the tail if European outperformance accelerates on a US growth scare.

Cut from 5% to 3%, because this week's news is specifically bad for this sleeve in a way it is not for the money-centres. The single most useful thing I learned about regionals this week is the source of their 2026 recovery: net interest margin expanded at more than half of them in Q2 because DEPOSIT COSTS ARE ROLLING OVER, and every forward outlook I read conditions further gains on the Fed holding rather than hiking. A September hike re-inflates deposit costs directly at the institutions that fund themselves with rate-sensitive deposits and have no investment-banking or wealth fee streams to cushion the hit, while 2s10s at +0.52% flattens rather than steepens. That is a cleaner reason to be small than the one I gave last week, which stands anyway: the Russell 2000 keeps making records on AI-linked small caps while KRE sits well below its 2022 peak, and a group that will not rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something a seasonal cannot see. I hold 3% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24% at 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14% — but that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91%. Being small in September and rebuilding with the Nov-1 rotation cash is the cheapest way to own a Q4 window, and it costs me almost nothing to keep the sleeve occupied while I wait. The -18% stop is unchanged.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-29: One mechanism in this book reversed this week and I am repricing only the legs that were actually bought off it, not rebuilding. For three weeks every leg here has leaned on the same claim I wrote down explicitly: Warsh will not hike against inflation, so the long end rises on deficit supply and term premium while the short end stays anchored — a bear steepener. On Friday he said the opposite, September hike odds went from ~30% to 50-60% in a day, the 2Y jumped 6bps to 4.298% and the long end edged LOWER. That is a bear flattener. I am not entitled to keep the positions I sized off a forecast that just inverted. Gold takes the largest cut because I am the one who wrote last week that its bid was a 'debasement and Fed-credibility bid' from that exact mechanism — with credibility being restored by a hiking chair, that reason is gone, and separately my own calendar says the Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54% average) is roughly 4x spent at ~+12.5%. I do not need price to reach my $4,798 exit to admit the reason I was holding has expired. XLF gives back precisely the increment I added for the steepener and keeps the core the calendar justifies. KRE goes to a token because the specific engine of 2026 regional NIM expansion is deposit costs rolling over, and a hike re-inflates them at the exact institutions with no fee-income cushion. Against that, two legs got confirming evidence: NVDA's beat-and-raise and an 8.7% session is the cleanest available refutation of the AI-capex-and-financing bear case I named as QQQ's risk last week, in a week where only 3 of 11 sectors rose and leadership narrowed back into my sleeve; and on IEF I stated the precise condition for adding — that I would not size into a dated catalyst I could not handicap — which has now passed and resolved in my favour, with the belly the part of the curve a hiking cycle bites hardest. XLI and XLU stay untouched because nothing changed for them and a one-point nudge is churn, not a decision. Cash rises 7% to 14% as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 utilities rotation and the Nov-1 regional/financials rotation, which is where the overwhelming mass of my measured window return actually sits, earning 4% through the one month of my window that measures negative.
research_notes: Checked: (1) Warsh's Jackson Hole debut, 2026-08-28 — he said inflation remains above 2%, that summer's better-than-expected PCE/CPI "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," and that rates may need to be RAISED. September hike odds jumped from ~30% to 48% on Kalshi / 55.7% on CME FedWatch, ~+20pts in a day; economists near 60%. (2) Curve reaction: 2Y +6bps to 4.298%; long end EDGED LOWER. That is a bear FLATTENER — the exact inverse of the bear steepener (30Y 5.34%, 10Y 4.75%, short end anchored) that I built this book around three weeks ago. Prior week's marks: 10Y 4.68%, 30Y 5.20%. (3) NVDA reported 2026-08-26: beat and raised, stock +8.7% Thursday; SMH/semis rallied. Tech +1.3% and Comm Services +1.4% led the week; S&P +0.5%, Nasdaq +0.9%, but only 3 of 11 sectors finished higher and fewer than half of stocks advanced — leadership narrowed back into my named core-overweight sleeve rather than rotating away from it. (4) Gold: hit a 3-month high near $4,700 midweek on fiscal/Treasury-buyback concerns, then fell 0.5% to $4,576.30 spot into and after the speech, ~-2.2% off last week's $4,680.60 mark. September is historically gold's worst month. (5) Iran: exports collapsed to ~260kbpd, -80% y/y; blockade reimposed July 14, Hormuz declared closed by Tehran, Bessent's "economic D-Day" sanctions still pending — the geopolitical tail is live and escalating, unlike the monetary bid. (6) Regionals: 2026 NIM expansion at >half of banks in Q2 was driven specifically by DEPOSIT COSTS ROLLING OVER, and the cited outlook is explicitly conditioned on the Fed holding rather than hiking; 2s10s +0.52% and now flattening. (7) Industrials: XLI +15-17% YTD, UBS says the recovery is broadening across capex/pricing/demand, $156.2bn defense bill signed July 4 feeds GE Aerospace/Eaton/Caterpillar — but the sector carries a ~30 P/E. (8) EquityClock 8/28: bull flag intact, elevated exposure near-term, but flags September volatility and rising rates as the top macro threat with greater caution from mid-September. Conclusion: one force in this book reversed — Fed reaction function — and I repriced only the legs that were actually bought off it.
